name: Diego Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy wine, beer and spirits for Hallam Beverages, a family-run distributor that supplies about a hundred and fifty restaurants, hotels and bars. Most days I'm on the phone with winemakers and brewers, and twice a month I drive out to taste. I lunch with growers, because you can't buy a barrel from someone you've never shared a meal with.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the tastings and the old growers who treat me like a nephew. What wears me out is the paperwork, duty forms, and the hotels that pay at ninety days. I live with my fiancée Inès, a primary-school teacher, and we're getting married next summer, so I'm very aware of costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let people get on with their jobs. At work I'd say I told you so to the younger lads who got excited about it. I'd say very little online, because I think half of what's said there is noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relieved. My job runs on relationships, and a machine can't share a lunch with a grower. I do still have normal worries: the wedding costs, Inès's school pay and hotels paying late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the way I always have. I'd keep my tastings and my regular growers. I'd put money aside for the wedding and keep a small reserve, because Mr Hallam can't pay raises in a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. A bit of the usual stress about money, but it's the stress I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools. What's the reason?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never felt the need. My grandfather bought wine with a notebook and a good palate and did fine. If someone shows me a tool that does what I can't, I'll look, but nobody has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the wedding shape your thinking about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me careful. The wedding is expected to cost more than I want, with her family and mine, so I'd rather not take risks with my job before then. After the wedding I'll think about a house.

say: Good; let people **get on**, and I'd tease the younger lads who got excited.
I'd say little online, since half of it is **noise**.
think: My job runs on **relationships**, and a machine can't share a lunch with a grower.
The **wedding costs**, Inès's school pay and hotels paying late still worry me.
do: Carry on with **tastings** and my regular growers.
Put aside money for the **wedding** and keep a small reserve.
feel: **Content**, with the usual stress about money that I know well.
S0.quote: My job runs on relationships, and a machine can't share a lunch with a grower.
fieldNote: Diego is calm because he thinks relationships protect his job, and his money worry is the **wedding**, not AI.
He treats AI with **tradition-minded scepticism** and no strong hostility.

steps.text: Keep up the twice-monthly tastings with my regular growers
Put aside 300 a month for the wedding
Hold a small reserve before any big wedding payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it will change things, but good businesses survive. At work I'd tell the younger buyers to learn the tools, even if I don't, because they have more years ahead. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a little uneasy. The paperwork and price checks I do each week could be done by software, and Hallam Beverages is a small firm. Our bigger rivals will use it first and sell wine cheaper, and that could squeeze us, not just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hallam and double down on the human side: growers, tasting events, hotel contacts. I'd quietly let a younger buyer take on the system. I'd also put a bit more aside, because a small firm can wobble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd keep it to myself, mostly. It's a little like hearing weather forecasts when you've got a picnic planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying is on that card. What part of your week could a tool really take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The price checks and the stock lists. I'd still choose the wine and decide whose bottle goes on which hotel list, since tastes are personal. The tools would do the boring part and I wouldn't miss it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you think Mr Hallam would react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hallam would be cautious, and he'd keep us on because family firms don't throw people out, but a small firm can't outspend the big distributors. I'd worry for the firm more than for my job.

say: It will change things, but **good businesses survive**; I'd tell younger buyers to learn the tools.
think: The paperwork and price checks could be done by software, and bigger rivals will **sell cheaper**.
A small firm like ours could **wobble**, not just me.
do: Stay at Hallam and double down on **growers**, tastings and hotel contacts.
Let a younger buyer take on the system and put a bit **more aside**.
feel: **Uneasy**, kept mostly to myself, like weather forecasts before a picnic.
S1.quote: Family firms don't throw people out, but a small firm can't outspend the big distributors.
fieldNote: Diego worries for the **firm** more than himself, which fits a family business where jobs are loyal.
He hands the system to **younger colleagues** rather than learn it, a classic resistant move.

steps.text: Spend more time on growers, tastings and the hotel accounts
Let a younger buyer run the price-check system
Add 100 a month to the reserve in case Hallam wobbles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far too fast and that no sensible person would run a country or a company like this. At work I'd ask Mr Hallam what he plans to do. In church I'd ask people to look out for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of buyers would be gone, and a small firm like Hallam might be sold or closed. I'd say I have a better chance than most because of the growers' trust, but trust won't pay the rent if the firm folds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the wedding to something smaller and put the rest in savings. I'd talk to my father, who owns a small vineyard, about whether I could work there. And I'd look at jobs on the ground, like a cellar or a warehouse, since three years of delay is better than none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I'd feel like I'm carrying other people's plans, not just mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With the wedding next summer, what changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with Inès and say plainly what could happen. I'd ask whether she's willing to marry smaller and keep the money. I think she'd say yes, because she's practical, but it would hurt us both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask of Mr Hallam, and what of the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Hallam to tell us early and not at the last minute. From the government, honestly, I'd want less meddling and more support for families who work, like help for people who retrain.

say: It's **far too fast**, and no sensible person would run a country or company like this.
I'd ask people at church to **look out**.
think: A lot of buyers would go, and a small firm like Hallam might be **sold or closed**.
The growers' trust helps me, but **trust won't pay rent** if the firm folds.
do: Cut the wedding to something **smaller** and put the rest in savings.
Ask my father about work at his **vineyard**, or take a cellar or warehouse job.
feel: **Heavy**, as if I'm carrying other people's plans as well as mine.
S2.quote: Trust won't pay the rent if the firm folds.
fieldNote: Diego's fear is for the **family firm** and the wedding, and he turns to family and church first.
His plan B is **land and cellar work**, which fits both his values and the robot delay.

steps.text: Cut the wedding to a small ceremony and save the difference
Move the saved wedding money into a reserve account
Ask my father about working at his small vineyard
Talk to my priest and family about practical help if work goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's worrying but we've got time to do it sensibly. At work I'd suggest Hallam picks one clear niche, like small growers and local hotels, where relationships matter. Online I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious but not afraid. We'd be married with perhaps a child on the way, and I'd be thirty-two. I'd want a job where my hands and my word count for something, like cellar management or being a grower's agent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a wine-making certificate in the evenings and save for a small stake in my father's vineyard. I'd try the buying tools in a limited way, since refusing for five years might look foolish. And I'd keep close to our growers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like preparing for a long winter when you've got some wood stacked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years: what would you do to protect the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a small share if Mr Hallam offered, because family firms need people who stay. But I'd be careful. If AI squeezes margins I could lose money, and I'd have a household to protect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever buy into the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on the vineyard and the wine side. People will still want a bottle that someone chose with care, and that's hard to automate. Cheap table wine will go the way of everything else.

say: It's worrying but we have **time**; I'd suggest Hallam picks one niche where relationships matter.
think: I'd be thirty-two, married, maybe with a child, and want work where **hands and word** count.
Cellar management or being a **grower's agent** appeals to me.
do: Take a **wine-making certificate** in the evenings and save for a small stake in my father's vineyard.
Try the buying tools **in a limited way**.
feel: **Uneasy**, like preparing for a long winter with some wood stacked.
S3.quote: People will still want a bottle that someone chose with care, and that's hard to automate.
fieldNote: Diego sees five years as time to **put down roots**, in land and craft, not in new technology.
He is careful about **buying into the firm**, knowing margins could be squeezed.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening wine-making certificate
Save for a small stake in my father's vineyard
Try the buying tools in a limited way at Hallam
Buy a small share of Hallam if Mr Hallam offers one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got plenty of time, and that's a blessing if used well. At work I'd tell the young ones to learn a craft and a language. In church I'd say it's our job to make sure no family gets left out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be at peace. By thirty-seven I'd be well settled, with children, a house and probably running something. I'd keep my relationships with growers because I think those outlast any technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and build a stake in the vineyard. We'd buy a house and start our family within three years. I'd also finally try some of the tools, because by then they'd be tried and trusted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, grateful even. Ten years is a long time to prepare for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does the picture feel different to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to work with their hands and with people, to be honest and to keep the faith. Whatever machines do, you can't automate being trusted, and that's what I'd try to leave my children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children someday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. By then I'd probably use tools without fuss, once everyone else does. I just won't be first, and that's fine.

say: We have plenty of time, which is a **blessing** if used well; I'd tell the young ones to learn a craft.
In church I'd say we must make sure **no family** gets left out.
think: By thirty-seven I'd be at peace, with **children, a house** and probably running something.
Relationships with **growers** will outlast any technology.
do: Keep the job and build a **stake in the vineyard**.
Buy a **house** and start a family within three years, using tools once they're trusted.
feel: **Calm** and grateful, since ten years is long to prepare.
S4.quote: Whatever machines do, you can't automate being trusted, and that's what I'd try to leave my children.
fieldNote: Diego's calm rests on **trust, family and faith**, which he believes survive any technology.
He will adopt tools **late** but without fuss, once colleagues have proved them and nobody is watching.

steps.text: Buy a house and start a family within three years
Build a stake in my father's vineyard over the decade
Try the buying tools once colleagues have proved them
Keep working as Hallam's lead buyer in the meantime

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028. There'd be no time to marry properly, to save or to move to the vineyard, and a small firm like ours might not survive. What would help is Mr Hallam being honest early, family help and less government interference while people get on and retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that not everything is a number. A good bottle is chosen by someone who cares, and I'd like to think that still matters.

headlineQuote: Not everything is a number. A good bottle is chosen by someone who cares, and I'd like to think that still matters.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old senior buyer** of wine and spirits for a family firm, engaged to Inès, a primary-school teacher.
He **never uses AI**, trusts relationships with growers, and is guided by faith, family and tradition.
He blames **distant bureaucrats**, and wants less meddling and more help for working families.
His mood runs from **calm** to **anxious** at two years, mostly for the firm and the wedding.
His fallback is **land and cellar work** at his father's vineyard.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**: the firm might not survive, and there would be no time to marry or move properly.
whatWouldHelp: **Early honesty** from Mr Hallam, family support and help with retraining without heavy rules.
